papers.title: Variable Bound Tightening for Nash Equilibrium Computation in Multiplayer Imperfect-Information Games
papers.abstract: There has been significant recent progress in algorithms for approximation of Nash equilibrium in large two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games and exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer strategic-form games. While counterfactual regret minimization and fictitious play are scalable to large games and have convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games, they do not guarantee convergence to Nash equilibrium in multiplayer games. Recently, an approach has been presented for exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer imperfect-information games that solves a quadratically constrained program based on a nonlinear complementarity problem formulation derived from the sequence-form game representation. This formulation was solved using Gurobi's nonconvex quadratic solver, which employs spatial branch-and-bound to iteratively refine variable bounds by solving convex relaxations of bilinear terms. During presolve, Gurobi introduces auxiliary variables and, in some cases, binary variables, leading to an internal mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. This approach was demonstrated to outperform prior algorithms from the Gambit software suite and quickly solve three-player Kuhn poker after removal of dominated actions; however, the algorithm was not able to solve the full version of the game within 24 hours. In this paper, we derive finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables in the nonlinear complementarity formulation. These bounds can strengthen the convex relaxations used within spatial branch-and-bound. We compare uniform corollary bounds with finer proposition-based bounds on full three-player Kuhn poker. All eight bounded configurations return numerically verified equilibria in under 17 seconds, while the unbounded formulation finds no feasible solution within 300 seconds. The finest bounds do not consistently yield the fastest computation.

papers.title: Stability and Perfection in Constrained Weighted Network Games
papers.abstract: We introduce a general framework of constrained weighted network formation in which agents allocate resources across coalitional interactions while facing feasibility constraints. More precisely, we allow arbitrary coalitions of agents to be assigned a continuous weight, and we incorporate both coalitional capacity constraints and individual budget constraints into the model. This framework extends the weighted network formation model of Bich and Morhaim by combining continuous interaction intensities with endogenous feasibility restrictions. Within this setting, we introduce a new notion of stability -- called coalitionwise stability -- extending pairwise stability to constrained network games. Under standard continuity and componentwise quasiconcavity assumptions on payoff functions, we establish the existence of coalitionwise stable networks. We then investigate refinements of stability inspired by the notion of perfect equilibrium introduced by Selten, and by the notion of perfect pairwise stability developed by Bich and Teteryatnikova for network games. The presence of feasibility constraints fundamentally alters the geometry of the feasible set, which no longer possesses a product structure. As a consequence, trembling-hand type refinements become substantially more delicate, since perturbations of some interactions may render other interactions infeasible. Nevertheless, we introduce constrained analogues of both the trembling-hand and perturbative notions of perfect stability considered by Bich and Teteryatnikova, and study their existence and their relationship. In particular, we show the equivalence between these trembling-hand and perturbative formulations under some componentwise monotonicity assumption.

papers.title: Iterated Elimination of Dominated Mixed Strategies
papers.abstract: This note compares two iterated dominance procedures, one based on eliminating mixed strategies and one based on eliminating pure strategies. It shows that, in compact and continuous games, the mixed-strategy procedure can trail the pure-strategy procedure by at most one round: If the pure-strategy procedure terminates at round $M$, the mixed-strategy procedure terminates at either $M$ or $M+1$, and this bound is tight. It also provides two characterizations of the mixed-strategy procedure that are round-for-round equivalent to it and that require checking for improvements only against opponents' pure strategies.

papers.title: Neural networks and games
papers.abstract: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

papers.title: Organizing Intelligence
papers.abstract: When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a model of how intelligence, the ability to achieve goals, matters for organizations, the key unit of economic production. Agents (human or AI) with multidimensional capabilities sort endogenously into competing firms. A firm's productivity depends on its agents' capabilities; we distinguish competence, which shifts productivity levels, from coordination, which governs how productivity scales with size. Two differences between AI and humans drive transformation: AI expertise is reproducible while humans' are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same human limits on coordination. We analyze how equilibrium market structure, productivity, employment, and wages evolve as AI capabilities improve. When AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordination improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated AI-heavy firms. Changes in human employment are gradual when AI displaces workers within mixed human-AI firms, or sudden when AI firms outcompete human firms. We decompose wage changes into a technology effect, which changes the value of humans within existing firms, and a reorganization effect as firms adjust size and composition. Reorganization can reverse the technology effect on wages.

papers.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design with Endogenous Information and Hidden Actions
papers.abstract: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design along two dimensions: joint endogeneity and interaction of hidden actions, information production, and disclosure; and generality across economic environments and feasibility structures. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect correlated Bayesian equilibrium, establish a dynamic revelation principle under this concept, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Focusing on a private-values environment allows us to characterize joint incentives through choice optimality, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, global integral monotonicity, and history-report incentives. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, conditional revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions and branched outcomes. We characterize feasible and optimal disclosure. Applications show the Milgrom-Weber revenue ranking can reverse with endogenous information acquisition, while optimal financial-contract disclosure may be absent, interior, or complete.

papers.title: Learning to Design Information
papers.abstract: Information designers, such as large language models and online platforms, often do not know the subjective beliefs of their receivers or users. We construct learning algorithms enabling the designer to learn the belief of a strategic receiver through repeated interactions. Our learning algorithms are robust to the receiver's strategic manipulation of the learning process of the designer. We study regret relative to two benchmarks to measure the performance of the algorithms. The static benchmark is $T$ times the single-period optimum for the designer under a known belief. The dynamic benchmark, which is stronger, characterizes global dynamic optimality for the designer under a known belief. Our learning algorithms allow the designer to achieve no regret against both benchmarks at fast convergence speeds of $O(\frac{\log^2 T}{T})$, significantly faster than other approaches in the literature.

papers.title: Optimality of Separate Selling with Finite-Support Values
papers.abstract: We characterize when separate selling is exactly revenue-optimal in multi-item auctions with additive buyers and independent, finitely supported valuations. For each item, the valuation distribution is identical across buyers, but it may differ across items. We show that, provided at least two items have a strictly positive non-top support value, separate selling is optimal for any number of buyers $n \ge 2$ if and only if top selling, which sells each item only at its highest possible value, is optimal for a single buyer. This equivalence holds under both dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and Bayesian incentive compatibility. We then characterize the optimality of top selling in the one-buyer problem through the existence of a particular class of dual flows and derive a necessary condition and several sufficient conditions on the value distributions for its optimality. These conditions reveal a common economic feature, which we call top-value isolation: high non-top valuations must be sufficiently far below the highest value or carry sufficiently little probability mass relative to the probability mass at the highest value.

papers.title: Weak Atomic Continuity and Subgame Perfection
papers.abstract: Subgame-perfect equilibrium need not exist in continuous games with perfect information when Nature moves. Under standard regularity assumptions, we prove that weak atomic continuity of Nature's transition probabilities yields a measurable pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium for finite and infinite horizons. The condition, originating in the population genetics literature, is necessary for the existence of subgame-perfect equilibrium uniformly over the remaining primitives: whenever this condition is violated, one can construct a dynamic game with no subgame-perfect equilibrium, even in behavioral strategies. The proof preserves compactness and upper hemicontinuity of continuation payoff correspondences under integration without requiring convexity.

papers.title: Universal Nonexistence of Monotone Equilibrium in Multiunit Auctions with Risk Aversion
papers.abstract: We establish universal nonexistence results for monotone pure-strategy equilibrium in multiunit auctions with risk-averse bidders. Fix any number of bidders greater than one and any profile of strictly increasing concave utilities, with at least one strictly risk-averse bidder. Under uniform pricing, for every supply of at least three units, we construct independent, full-support type distributions under which neither lowest-winning-bid nor highest-losing-bid pricing admits an admissible monotone equilibrium. Under discriminatory pricing, we construct a finite supply and independent, full-support type distributions that preclude monotone pure-strategy equilibrium. We extend these results to all-pay auctions and finite bid grids.

papers.title: Inventory and Assortment Optimization under General Choice: A Unified Approximation Framework
authors: Jacob Feldman (Washington University in St. Louis)
papers.abstract: We study joint inventory and assortment optimization under general substitutable choice models. Before a selling horizon, a decision maker chooses initial inventories subject to a capacity constraint on total units stocked, and customers then arrive sequentially and choose among the offered products. We consider two settings, show-all inventory selection, in which every in-stock product must be offered, and dynamic assortment personalization, in which the decision maker observes each customer's type and may adapt the offered assortment to remaining inventory and purchase history. We develop a unified framework linking each setting to a static optimization problem. For show-all inventory selection, a polynomial-time $\alpha$-approximation for cardinality-constrained static assortment optimization yields guarantees of $0.486\alpha$ under deterministic or Poisson arrivals and $0.4328\alpha$ under increasing-failure-rate (IFR) arrivals. For personalization, the same guarantees hold when $\alpha$ is the approximation factor for the joint assortment and customization problem of El Housni and Topaloglu. Our approach combines a fluid relaxation, demand-dependent fractional inventory allocations, bounds on expected truncated demand, and dependent rounding. Notably, our personalized policy fixes one assortment per customer type before the horizon and then offers every in-stock product within it, so it requires no dynamic re-optimization despite competing against the optimal fully adaptive policy. Finally, we construct instances in which optimal show-all revenue approaches only one-half of the fluid bound under deterministic arrivals and $1-w\approx0.4328567$ under IFR arrivals, where $we^w=1$. With an exact static assortment oracle, our IFR guarantee approaches the latter factor arbitrarily closely.

papers.title: A Bulow-Klemperer Theorem for Bundling and Improved Approximation Bounds for Simple Auctions
papers.abstract: We study simple auctions for one additive bidder whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for the optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the optimal revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for the grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{BSPA}_2 \le 2\,\mathrm{BREV}$. Thus, one additional bidder lets a reserve-free second-price auction for the grand bundle match the optimal revenue from one bidder, regardless of the number of items. This gives a Bulow-Klemperer theorem for bundling and resolves an open question of Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, and Weinberg (EC 2025) on whether constant competition suffices for bundling. The factor-$2$ bundling approximation is also tight. For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{\pi^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). For the lower bound, we construct an instance in which pricing three disjoint bundles earns more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). Together, these results narrow the tight approximation ratio to the range $[2.11, 2.645]$.

papers.title: Robust Tournaments
papers.abstract: We characterize robust tournament design---the prize scheme that maximizes the lowest equilibrium effort in a rank-order tournament where the distribution of noise is unknown, except for an upper bound, $\bar{H}$, on its Shannon entropy. The robust tournament awards positive prizes to all ranks except the last, with a distinct top prize. Robust prizes spread marginal incentives as evenly as possible across performance quantiles, minimizing the Kullback--Leibler divergence from the uniform distribution to the induced distribution of performance cutoffs. Asymptotically, robust prizes follow the harmonic number sequence, while the worst-case distribution of noise converges to an exponential distribution with rate $e^{1-\bar{H}}$. The prize scheme is highly unequal, especially in small tournaments, but becomes more equitable as the number of agents grows, with the Gini coefficient approaching $1/2$. In the large tournament model, logarithmic prizes and an exponential worst-case distribution also arise under a bound on expected noise above the lower endpoint of its support, and more generally under bounds on a class of means of the quantile hazard.

papers.title: Randomization and ambiguity perception
papers.abstract: Ambiguity-averse decision makers typically dislike not only the presence of ambiguous events but also their increase, contrary to what standard ambiguity models predict. We axiomatically study such a decision maker. She avoids ex ante randomization over prospects since it increases the number of relevant ambiguous events without providing a hedge against uncertainty. Our axioms lead to a representation in which the decision maker behaves as if she optimizes her ambiguity perception at a cost. We show the uniqueness of the representation and conduct comparatives of attitudes toward ambiguity and its increase. This identification is not achieved without considering ex ante randomization.

papers.title: Separating the Wheat from the Chaff
papers.abstract: We study a reputational cheap-talk environment in which a judge chooses between two speakers of unknown expertise, an expert and a quack. Both speakers seek to be selected, while the judge wishes to identify the expert. The best equilibrium for the judge features truth-telling by the expert, yet the judge favors speakers with more extreme messages. This bias toward extremism does not induce exaggeration, but instead sustains truthful communication. We characterize the quack's equilibrium messaging strategy, relating the degree to which it panders to the judge's prior to the state distribution, the speakers' initial reputations, and the judge's private knowledge of the state. We interpret these results in the context of two applications, the post-training of AI chatbots through human feedback and media competition.

papers.title: Solving Problems of Unknown Difficulty
papers.abstract: This paper studies how uncertainty about problem difficulty shapes problem-solving strategies. I develop a dynamic model where an agent solves a problem by brainstorming approaches of unknown quality and allocating a fixed effort budget among them. Success arrives from spending effort pursuing good approaches, at a rate determined by the unknown problem difficulty. The agent balances costly exploration (expanding the set of approaches) with exploitation (pursuing existing approaches). Failures could signal either a bad idea or a hard problem, and this uncertainty generates novel dynamics: optimal search alternates between trying new approaches and revisiting previously abandoned ones. I then examine a principal-agent environment, where moral hazard arises on the intensive margin: how the agent explores. Dynamic commitment creates a frontloading force, which can be counteracted by the presence of learning. The framework reflects scientific discovery, product development, and other creative work, providing insights into innovation and organizational design.
